content.text: Where the largest shard of the comet Vhezar fell. Glass dunes, ember geysers, and the ruins of the old capital. Nothing grows here but firemoss and grudges.
A jungle valley that swallowed three kingdoms after the Fall. The canopy glows faintly at night — spores from the ember-changed trees.
Mountains where the dead of the Fall were carried for burial. The passes are safe by day. By night the fog remembers names.
The only coastline spared by the Fall, now choked with refugees' descendants, trade houses, and smugglers' fleets.
The great port and de facto capital of the after-world. Paper lanterns, ink-stained clerks, and the Ledger-Court that rules by contract law.
A fortress-city built into the cooled crater wall. Its founders mine the comet-glass; its children are born with grey eyes.
A city grown rather than built — houses trained from living banyan, streets that shift a finger-width every year.
The pilgrim city at the crater's edge, where the Emberfaith keeps its eternal forge-shrines.
Terraced granite city of the mountain clans, keepers of the funerary roads and the toll-gates on every pass.
A floating bazaar lashed together from a thousand hulls. Anything can be bought; most of it was stolen.
The last city before the high fogs, built around a well that never freezes and never empties.
A river-ford village of eel-farmers and toll-takers.
Sheep, slate, and silence. The harrowstones hum before avalanches.
Glass-farmers who harvest the dunes by starlight, when the sand cools.
A shore village famous for wind-carved whistling cliffs and unlicensed salvage.
Built in the ribcage of some vast Fall-killed beast, now furred green.
The village at the base of the funerary roads. Every family digs.
The drowned senate-hall of the old kingdom, its debate still audible at low tide, word for word, a century stale.
The mine that dug too close to the buried shard. Its tunnels are now grown with comet-glass that dreams.
A monastery library whose books were chained to stop them leaving. After the Fall, the chains were needed.
The overgrown court of the Green Queen, swallowed in a single night of growth.
A free-standing arch of fused glass at the crater's exact center. Nothing that walks through it on the ember-tide returns unchanged.
The comet-watcher's flagship, thrown a mile inland by the Fall's wave, still burning a cold blue light in its crow's nest.
The comet itself, worshipped and cursed in equal measure. Its clergy argue whether the Fall was judgment, accident, or invitation.
Goddess of the space between places. Every crossroads shrine holds a coin no one dares spend.
The Verdant Throat's slow god. Prayers are planted, not spoken, and answered in seasons.
A mortal clerk deified by common consensus in Vellum Reach. His miracle: a debt, once written fairly, cannot be unjustly enforced.
Keeper of the funerary roads. Counts every name the fog remembers, and forgets none itself.

content.text: Mercenaries who only take contracts written under Saint Ledger's seal.
Founded in the hungry decades after the Fall, the The Grey Company now shapes the politics of the after-world.

Ivex Callo signs nothing she has not read twice and forgives nothing she has signed. She rose from harbor-clerk to Chancellor in nineteen years, on the strength of a single audited ledger that hanged three trade princes.
Rumor holds she keeps Saint Ledger's original quill, and that it writes one true sentence a year.

Sella tends the eternal forges with burn-scarred hands and a patience that frightens younger clergy. She preaches that the Fall was a lantern lowered to a dark world — and that lanterns can be lowered twice.
Douro has walked every funerary road twice and paid the fog-toll once, which is once more than most survive. He does not speak of what name the fog took from him in payment.
It was his own; the man now answers to a borrowed one.

Mirren was planted — their word — as an infant beneath the banyan court and raised by the Choir. They translate the jungle's slow intentions into fast human words, and are never wrong, and never entirely on anyone's side.
Coa Brack owns a hundred ships on paper and three hundred off it. She learned accounting from pirates and piracy from accountants, and considers the distinction sentimental.
Pell dives the Sunken Rotunda with wax-sealed ears so the old debates cannot argue him into staying. His recovered folios rebuilt half of contract law. His nightmares recite the other half.
Oruna shaped the first pane of dreaming glass and has refused every offer to shape another. The Union follows her because she alone knows which veins of the Deep may be safely cut.
No one remembers Brother Tallow young. He repairs bridges, marries travelers, buries the road's dead, and carries in his coin-purse a single coin that every shrine of Mother Meridian refuses.
The coin is the first toll ever paid, and it is looking for its way home.
Erya reads every contract aloud to her company before a single sword is drawn, and has broken exactly one — the clause is framed above her desk, crossed out in her own blood.

Something walked back out of the Ember Gate wearing the old king's face, a century after the old king died. It is charming, patient, generous to the poor — and it wants every ember of Vhezar gathered in one place. The Ashen Hand calls it majesty.
The Pale Auditor's ledgers list the Kindled King as an unpaid debt.

Sarl harvests dune-glass like his mothers before him, except his harvest shows tomorrow's weather in its facets, and lately, other tomorrows. The village keeps his gift quiet. Three factions already suspect. This season the facets have begun showing a door.
Every secret in Brinemarket passes through the Nightingale's rookery of trained fog-crows. Her prices are strange: a memory, a habit, one hour of someone's name.

The first toll ever paid to Mother Meridian. Whoever carries it always finds the road they need, never the road they want.
A short sword that cannot cut anyone who has kept every promise they made. It has never once failed to cut.
The first and only sheet of dreaming comet-glass. Sleepers near it share one dream, and lately the dream has a doorway in it.
A fist-sized fragment of the comet's heart, still falling in some direction no compass names. The Ashen Hand has gathered eleven. This is the twelfth.
Rung once, it tells you if a dead name has been collected by the fog. Rung twice, it tells the fog where you are.
A book listing every secret its owner has ever sold — and, on the facing pages, what each buyer did with it.
Bone whistle that calls one specific crow, who decides whether to answer.
Tide-tables for the crater's glass dunes; wrong twice a year, fatally.
Its chain is newer than the book. Someone re-shackled it after the Fall.
A coin no one dares spend. Standard issue at every crossroads.
Sheet music. The Deep's glass veins split cleanly along the third harmony.
Proof of passage, stamped by Brother Tallow. Older ones are collector's items.
Grave-iron disc; the fog honors it, mostly.
Still bangs itself once at low tide, calling a session no one attends.
A prayer written on a seed-husk. Planting it is the asking.
Forty clauses, Saint Ledger's seal, and one blank line that fills itself in.
Woven fog-grey. The dead cannot see through it; the living should not try.
Burns the same cold blue as the flagship's crow's nest. Never lit by hand.
The comet Vhezar broke apart in the high dark and fell across a night that lasted three days. Every calendar of the after-world counts from this.

date.value: Year 0, third day of the Fall

content.text: The Fall's wave took the senate mid-debate. The motion on the floor — evacuation — had just failed by two votes.
The roads after the Fall were not safe until someone paid for them. What Brother Tallow paid is not recorded. The roads have been passable since.
Refugee clerks, lacking a king, ruled that a fair contract outranks a crown. It has held for eighty-eight years.
The Union won sole rights to the Deep in exchange for sealing whatever had started singing back.
The Green Queen's palace vanished under jungle in one night. The Choir insists it was mercy.
The Queen's dinner guests are, by some accounts, still dining.
For one night the mountain fog spoke every name it had collected, in order. Cairnfoot transcribed 4,411 of them before dawn.
A hundred smuggler captains agreed on exactly one law: the market itself is neutral ground. Violations to date: three. Survivors of violations: none.
On the ember-tide of Year 89, the Gate lit from the inside, and the old king walked out smiling. He remembered everyone's name. That was the frightening part.
The Ashen Hand breached the sealed gates and left with a lead-wrapped burden. The Union resealed the Deep and doubled the choir of cutting-songs.
For nine days no secrets moved in Brinemarket. When the rookery reopened, every price had changed, and the Nightingale had a new scar shaped like a keyhole.
The Auditor came down from the fogs to count something in Duskwell. It counted, thanked the town politely, and left. The well has been three degrees warmer since.
What it counted was doors.
Eleven embers gathered, one stolen, and the twelfth on the Kindled King's person. The Ledger-Court drafts contingencies. The Emberfaith prays for a lantern. The Ashen Hand prays for a second Fall.
